newsitem.title: ROMANIA: IMF starts new loan talks with Romania.
newsitem.headline: IMF starts new loan talks with Romania.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has started talks with Romania's new centrist ruling coalition aimed at resuming Fund credits suspended last year.

Visiting IMF negotiator Poul Thomsen met Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea before talks on a new standby deal, expected to underpin a package of macroeconomic stabilisation and economic reforms, a government statement said on Wednesday.

"It's a programme that emphasises stabilisation and reform, plus accompanying social programmes to alleviate the impact on groups that will be most affected," Thomsen told reporters after Wednesday's meeting with Ciorbea.

The talks, expected to continue over the next three weeks, will fine-tune the details of Romania's monetary, fiscal and budget policies for 1997, as well as plans to speed up restructuring and privatisation of state-owned companies.

"I'm particularly pleased that it's an integrated, consistent....sustainable and realistic approach," said Thomsen, without giving further details on the reform package, which is expected to include price and foreign exchange market liberalisation, coupled with social protection steps.
"We agreed to finalise those negotiations in the first days of February," Ciorbea told reporters.
He said the talks with the IMF would proceed in parallel to negotiations with World Bank, European Union and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) experts.
There was no breakdown for the amount of financial assistance which Romania seeks from those institutions.

"Any delay in implementing the (reform) programme would trigger negative consequences, both on the economic and social level," said Ciorbea, whose centrist coalition removed leftists from office in last November's elections.
The Fund suspended a previous $460 million three-year standby deal in 1996, over foreign exchange market curbs and overspending by the former leftists in an electoral year.
One month ago an IMF mission judged that Romania had sunk into an economic crisis grimmer than previously thought.
Latest data show year-on-year inflation soared to 56.9 percent in 1996, almost triple the IMF's 20 percent target.
The 1996 budget deficit rose to 5.7 percent of gross domestic product from initial pledges of 2.2 percent, with the current account deficit expected to hit $2.0 billion.

Cutting budget spending, restore free exchange markets and restructure energy-intensive and farming industries are planks which would help the Balkan country to win Fund approval for renewed credits. -- Roxan Dascalu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 31202
